en: The Legend of the Elder Adhimutta Kuṇḍadhāna Chapter, Number Six I was once a king named Mahinda, ruling over the entire earth. At that time, the Buddha Kassapa, the Great Sage, appeared in the world. Having heard of his arrival, I went to him with a great retinue. Having approached the Teacher, I paid homage at his feet. Then, having offered alms-food to the Teacher, I sat down to one side. Seated there, I spoke these words to the Teacher, the Conqueror: "O Blessed One, I wish to go forth; please grant me ordination. The Teacher, the Great Sage, granted me the going-forth and the full admission. Having gone forth under the Teacher, I practiced the holy life. For eighty-four thousand years I maintained the practice of celibacy. When the Teacher had passed away, I became a monk endowed with supernormal powers. I dwelt in the Himalayas, practicing meditation in the forest. There I saw a deer, a doe, giving birth to a fawn. Seeing her suffering in pain, I felt compassion for her. I then took up a blade of grass and placed it in her mouth. Because of that act of merit, I have been reborn in heaven. From that time on, I have always been born in the realm of the gods. Now, having fallen from that state, I have been reborn here in the human world. I am now an elder named Adhimutta, dwelling in the city of Sāvatthī. I am a monk who has attained the fruit of Arhatship. I have reached the end of suffering and am free from all defilements. This is my own legend, told in brief. May all beings be well and happy. May they live long and enjoy prosperity. May they be free from all suffering. May they attain the supreme bliss of Nibbāna. Thus ends the legend of the Elder Adhimutta.
“When Atthadassī, the supreme among men, the Protector of the World, had entered Nibbāna,
I attended upon the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.”
With a serene mind,
having invited the Saṅgha of bhikkhus—
upright and concentrated.
Having constructed a pavilion of sugarcane,
I fed the supreme Saṅgha.
Whichever womb I am reborn into, [I shall be honored].
Whether divine or human,
I overcome all beings;
this is the fruit of meritorious action.
In eighteen hundred kappas,
because of the gift I gave then,
I have not known a miserable rebirth.
This is the fruit of giving sugarcane.
[I possess] the four analytical knowledges... [and so on].
“Thus was the teaching of the Buddha spoken.
In this way, the venerable elder Adhimutta indeed spoke these verses.
This is the sixth legend of the elder Adhimutta.
